standard: CCSS HSG-SRT.C.6: Understand that by similarity, side ratios in right triangles are properties of the angles in the triangle, leading to definitions of trigonometric ratios for acute angles.
source: Original content written for Pip (no third-party text copied); aligned to CCSS HSG-SRT.C.6.
attribution: Pip team, original. The Common Core State Standards are cited for alignment only (c) NGA Center / CCSSO.
in_scope: sine as opposite over hypotenuse (given: Pip knows the definition)
triangles with the same angles being scaled copies
opposite and hypotenuse scaling together so their ratio stays the same
using sin 30° = 0.5 to find a side
ramps, zoomed photos and shadows as pictures of scaling
out_of_scope: cosine and tangent as their own mission
law of sines and law of cosines
exact values for angles other than 30, 45 and 60 degrees

look_fors: Says triangles with the same angles are the same shape, just zoomed in or out (one sentence is enough)
Says the angles do not change when the triangle is scaled
May use a photo, a mini ramp and a big ramp, or a scaled copy as the picture
probe_ladder: why is that wrong? when i make my 30° triangle bigger its sine gets bigger, i checked.
if i zoom my 30° triangle to twice the size, do the angles change?
is the big triangle a different shape from the small one, or something else?
then a 30° triangle the size of a house has a house-sized sine. that's what my rule says.
concrete: what if i zoom a photo of my triangle to twice the size, what happens to its angles?
connections: so it's like zooming a photo, the picture gets bigger but nothing inside it bends?
so it's like a mini ramp and a huge ramp that tilt the exact same way?
concepts.friend_nudge: My cousin said a mini ramp and a huge ramp can tilt the exact same amount…? I don't know what that has to do with sine.
concepts.aha: ohh so the big one is just my small one blown up.
idea_patterns: angles? (stay|stays|don'?t change|doesn'?t change|are the same|is the same|equal)

look_fors: Says the opposite side and the hypotenuse both get multiplied by the same amount when the triangle is scaled
So the ratio opposite ÷ hypotenuse stays the same
May show it with numbers: 3/6 and 6/12 are both 0.5
probe_ladder: what happens to the opposite side and the hypotenuse when i double the triangle?
if my small one has opposite 3 and hypotenuse 6, what are they in the doubled one?
what is opposite divided by hypotenuse in the small one, and in the doubled one?
then a bigger triangle has a bigger sine, because the numbers got bigger. that's what my rule says.
concrete: what if i double both numbers, 3 and 6, what do i get for 3 divided by 6, and for 6 divided by 12?
connections: so it's like a pizza and a bigger pizza cut the same way, same fraction per slice?
so it's like a pole and its shadow both getting longer together?
concepts.friend_nudge: My neighbor said if you double a whole recipe, how it tastes stays put…? I'm not sure what she meant.
concepts.aha: ok so both sides grow together and the ratio just sits there.

look_fors: Uses sin 30° = 0.5 to find a side: 10 × 0.5 = 5
Applies it to a new size (a different hypotenuse) without recomputing the ratio
Says when it applies: any right triangle with that angle
probe_ladder: if the ramp is 10 ft long along the slope and the angle is 30°, how high does it rise?
what if the ramp were 20 ft long at the same 30° tilt?
i'll guess a 10 ft ramp at 30° rises 10 ft, same as its length. is that right?
then a 20 ft ramp at 30° rises 20 ft times a bigger sine. that's what my rule says.
concrete: what if i build a 10 ft ramp at 30°, how tall is the top?
connections: so it's like a skate ramp, any size at that tilt rises the same share of its length?
concepts.friend_nudge: Someone in my class said a flagpole and its shadow always match up the same way at the same sun angle…? I don't get how that helps.
concepts.aha: ok so at 30° the ramp always rises that fixed share of its length.
